title: Fossil fuel limits cut from latest draft of UN climate deal
summary: Climate negotiators stripped out any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels in a slimmed-down draft deal text published on Thursday, as ‌the COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, approaches its…

image.caption: Members of 350.org attend a boxing-themed demonstration calling for an electrification target based on renewable energy, not fossil fuels, at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 19. (REUTERS)

blocks.text: Climate negotiators stripped out any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels in a slimmed-down draft deal text published on Thursday, as ‌the COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, approaches its Friday deadline.
Draft acknowledges 'deep, rapid and sustained cuts' to greenhouse gas emissions needed
The first draft published on Monday had contained two references to fossil fuels and limiting their use — ​a topic that deeply divides nations in the ​negotiations every year.
The draft acknowledged that global warming could exceed the 1.5 C threshold countries have ​sought to preserve and the need for "deep, rapid ⁠and sustained" cuts ⁠to greenhouse gas emissions.
It also ‌encouraged efforts to scale up the deployment of technologies that can suck carbon out of the atmosphere.
Who pays when climate disasters strike?

Australia, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement with Turkey, ⁠previously said Monday's opening draft of the deal was always intended to be a broad document that would then be narrowed down.
The ‌latest text is expected to be revised further before it can be agreed.

While the conference is scheduled to end on Friday, efforts in recent years to secure consensus among ​the nearly 200 countries participating have regularly blown past this deadline by more than ⁠24 hours.
The need to limit rising global temperatures is widely accepted ⁠by participants, but they don't all agree on the ⁠best way ⁠to do so, who ​should pay for it and how quickly the world needs to ​act.

The talks are ⁠taking place at a time when the warming climate and its increasingly severe and regular effects — including heat waves, floods and droughts — are competing for attention among policymakers and the public with war and rising living ⁠costs.
